meta.subject: Multipath geometry, virtual anchors, incidence points, and bounce-count inference

slides.notes: Open with the conversion problem: an MPC tuple is not yet a bounce count. The presentation moves through three knowledge regimes and makes each geometric construction operable on the following live slide.

elements.html: Turn delay, AoA, AoD, and complex MPC gain into a physically valid route—under progressively weaker geometric knowledge.
\(\tau\) · \(\varphi\) · \(\psi\) · \(\alpha\)

slides.notes: Define the resolved path tuple. Use the right-hand scene as three separate route examples—not three explanations of one measured tuple. Each reflected route is constructed with the image-source method, so incidence and reflection angles match at every wall contact. After synchronization and hardware-delay calibration, delay becomes path length. AoA and AoD must use explicit UE/BS array-frame conventions, and the calibrated complex MPC gain remains radiometric evidence rather than a direct bounce counter.

elements.html: One resolved path gives four observables
Geometry starts with delay and bearings; power helps distinguish otherwise similar routes.

delay \(\tau\) → \(L=c(\tau-\delta_\tau)\); synchronized: \(\delta_\tau=0\)
AoA \(\varphi\) → arrival bearing in the UE frame
AoD \(\psi\) → departure bearing in the BS frame
\(\alpha\in\mathbb C\) → complex MPC gain; \(|\alpha|^2\) → power gain

slides.notes: Read the power-delay profile from left to right. Each resolvable peak contributes one tuple; components inside the delay resolution remain superposed. The calibrated power gain from the squared magnitude of the complex MPC gain can penalize implausible material, roughness, interaction-count, or blockage hypotheses. Power supports geometry; it does not replace it.

elements.html: When delay-resolved, the PDP separates paths
Delay resolves candidate routes into peaks. Relative power adds evidence about their physical plausibility.
each interaction often adds loss—not a strict ordering
reflection loss depends on the surface
diffuse scattering weakens the specular path
occlusion can remove an otherwise valid route
Geometry proposes the route. Calibrated radiometry helps rank competing, geometrically valid routes.
